Name order refers to the sequence in which given names and family names appear in a person's full name, and it varies dramatically across cultures. The Western convention that most English speakers take for granted—given name first, family name last—is not universal at all.

Western European and North American tradition places the given name first and the family name last, like John Smith. But this became dominant through European colonial influence. It is not the default globally. East Asian cultures, including China, Japan, Korea, and Vietnam, traditionally place the family name first, then given names. Confucius's name was Kong Fuzi, where Kong is the family name. Hungarian and some Slavic cultures also reverse the Western order, putting family name first, though speakers sometimes drop this convention when they adopt Western naming in English-language contexts.

Many databases and forms assume Western name order, and this causes real errors when processing names from cultures with different conventions. A Vietnamese person named Nguyễn Văn A is often incorrectly indexed under "Văn" or "A" by systems expecting the family name to come last.

Some cultures don't have a concept of "family name" in the Western sense at all. Many Indigenous cultures, some African traditions, and Arab cultures have patronymic or clan systems that function completely differently. The confusion gets worse when scholars transliterate names. Classical Chinese and Japanese names often require context to parse correctly. Is "Zhang Wei" a given name or a family name? You need to know the tradition.
